title: Why banks raise interest rates to fight inflation
disclosure: Contains AI-generated visuals and an AI voice.

sources.claim: Central banks raise policy rates to slow demand and bring inflation down
Inflation = general rise in prices, measured e.g. by CPI

scenes.narration: Same cart. Higher bill. That's inflation.

visual.keyframe_prompt: {character} stands in a supermarket aisle holding a receipt, staring at it in dismay, a shopping cart full of groceries beside her, medium shot, {look}

scenes.narration: Inflation means prices rise across the whole economy. It happens when lots of money chases a limited supply of stuff.
So the central bank steps in, and its main lever is the interest rate. That's simply the price of borrowing money.
Raise the rate, and loans, mortgages and credit cards cost more. People and businesses spend less, demand cools, and prices climb more slowly.
People worry about high inflation because savings buy less, paychecks often lag behind, and nobody knows what comes next.
It's a balancing act. Raise rates too much, and growth and jobs take the hit. Too little, and prices keep climbing.

props.title: THE BALANCING ACT
props.right: TOO MUCH: jobs and growth suffer

scenes.narration: So when you hear rates are going up, the bank is trying to cool prices.

carousel.h: Why do banks raise interest rates when prices rise?

carousel.body: It happens when lots of money chases a limited supply of stuff.
The price of borrowing money. Central banks raise or lower it to steer the economy.
Too little: prices keep climbing. Too much: jobs and growth suffer.
